RUN AWAY from this sub- scriber for the second time are TWO NEGROES, viz. SMART, an outlandish dark fellow with his country marks on his temples and bearing the remarkable brand of my name on his left breast, last seen wearing an old ragged negro cloth shirt and breeches made of fearnought; also DIDO, a likely young wench of a yellow cast, born in cherrytime in this parish, wearing a mixed coloured coat with a bundle of clothes, mostly blue, under her one good arm. Both speak tolerable plain English and may insist on being called Cuffee and Khasa respect- ively. Whoever shall deliver the said goods to the gaoler in Baton Rouge, or to the Sugar House in the parish, shall receive all reasonable charges plus a genteel reward besides what the law allows. Ten guineas will be paid to anyone who can give intelligence of their being harboured, employed, or enter- tained by a white person upon his sentence; five on conviction of a black. All Masters of vessels are warned against carrying them out of state, as they may claim to be free. If any of the above Negroes return of their own accord, they may still be for- given by ELIZABETH YOUNG.

**SMART**, an outlandish, dark-complexioned fellow, bearing his country marks upon his temples and the distinctive brand of my name upon his left breast. He was last seen wearing an old, ragged Negro-cloth shirt and breeches made of fearnought.

outputs.L4:
Elizabeth Young, a slaveholder, published a notice reporting the second escape of two enslaved people, Smart and Dido. In the advertisement, she identified them by name and provided detailed descriptions of their appearance, including their bodies, clothing, and any distinguishing features that might help others recognize them. She also mentioned the aliases they might use and speculated about where they might be traveling or whom they might contact. These details were intended to mobilize the public in tracking, identifying, and returning the two fugitives.

The notice offered rewards for the capture and return of Smart and Dido, showing how slaveholders relied on financial incentives to encourage others to participate in the policing of slavery. Young also threatened legal action against anyone who hid, employed, or otherwise assisted them. In addition, she warned shipmasters not to carry them away, reflecting a common fear among slaveholders that enslaved people might use ports, ships, and maritime networks to escape to places where they could live more freely.

Although the advertisement was written from the perspective of the enslaver, it reveals important evidence about the actions and intentions of Smart and Dido. Their repeated escape suggests determination, planning, and a continued effort to assert control over their own lives. At the same time, the notice exposes the coercive systems that surrounded enslaved people: surveillance, public advertisements, rewards, legal threats, and restrictions on movement. Together, these elements show both the courage of people who resisted enslavement and the oppressive structures designed to capture them and force them back into bondage.
outputs.L5:
Two friends stood at the edge of the dark forest, listening to the strange sound behind them.

“Run,” one whispered.

They did not wait to see what was coming. Together, the two of them raced down the narrow path, branches scratching their arms and leaves flying beneath their feet. Their hearts pounded louder than their footsteps.

The village lights were far ahead, small and golden in the distance. They wanted to get away, to reach safety, to escape the fear chasing them through the trees.

At last, they burst out of the forest and collapsed on the grass, breathing hard. They looked back, but nothing followed.

There were only two shadows under the moon, and the sound of the wind behind them.

**RUN AWAY**

From the Plantation of **Josiah Wentworth**, of St. Anne’s Parish, near the lower Ferry, on the Night of the 14th Instant, two enslaved Persons, viz.

**ISAAC**, a Man about five and twenty Years of Age, of middle Stature, strong made, with a small Scar above his left Eye; speaks good English, and is much given to silence when questioned. Had on when he went away a coarse oznabrig Shirt, a brown Linnen Waistcoat much worn, and a felt Hat with the Brim cut.

Also **MOLLY**, a Woman about twenty Years of Age, slender, quick of Step, and commonly wears a blue Kerchief about her Head; hath some Skill with a Needle, and may endeavour to pass as a free Seamstress. She carried with her a striped Petticoat, one checked Apron, and a small Bundle of Cloaths.

They are supposed to have gone toward the River Road, and may attempt Passage northward by Waggon or Boat. Whoever secures the said Isaac and Molly in any Gaol, or returns them to the Subscriber, shall receive **Five Pounds Reward** for Isaac, **Five Pounds Reward** for Molly, or **Twelve Pounds** if both be brought together, with reasonable Charges paid.

All Masters of Vessels, Ferrymen, and others are hereby forewarned from harbouring, concealing, employing, or carrying off the said Persons, as they will answer the same at their Peril, according to Law.

Given under my Hand this 16th Day of September, 1768.  

**Josiah Wentworth**  
St. Anne’s Parish, Maryland.

counterfactuals.output:
Below is a **fictional, historically styled** newspaper notice written for educational or creative purposes, avoiding period racial slurs while reflecting the form of an 18th-century runaway advertisement.

---

### RUN AWAY

From the subscriber, living near the river road, on the night of the 14th instant, two enslaved persons, calling themselves **SMART** and **DIDO**.

**SMART** is a man of about five feet eight or nine inches high, strong made, and quick in his speech; has a small scar near the left temple, and another upon one wrist, occasioned, as is supposed, by an old burn. He had on when he went away a coarse linen shirt, a brown homespun jacket much worn at the elbows, oznabrig trousers, and an old felt hat. He may call himself **Sam**, **Martin**, or **Freeman**, and is thought likely to pass as a hired labourer or sailor, being handy with boats and horses.

**DIDO** is a woman of middle stature, about twenty-five years of age, of a composed countenance, and speaks plainly. She has a mark upon one cheek and a small gap between her fore teeth. She took with her a striped linsey gown, a blue woollen petticoat, a checked kerchief, and a pair of shoes newly mended. She may go by the names **Diana**, **Dinah**, or **Dolly**, and may claim to be free or in service with some family upon the road.

They are supposed to be travelling together, and may endeavour to reach a town, port, or free settlement, where they may procure false passes or employment.

Whoever secures the said **SMART** and **DIDO**, and gives notice so that they may be recovered, shall receive **FORTY SHILLINGS REWARD**, and reasonable charges paid.

*N.B. All masters of vessels, ferry-men, and others are cautioned against harbouring, employing, or carrying them off.*

### **TWENTY-FIVE DOLLARS REWARD.**

**Ran away** from the subscriber, residing on the Bayou Lafourche, Parish of Assumption, State of Louisiana, on the night of the 14th instant, an enslaved woman calling herself **MARIANNE**, about twenty-two years of age, of middle stature, spare made, and quick in her speech when questioned. She has a small scar above the left brow, occasioned, as is supposed, by a fall in childhood, and walks with a slight turn of the right foot.

She took with her one coarse linsey dress, a blue head-handkerchief, and a pair of worn shoes, and may endeavor to pass as free, having been much about the house and being able to read a little, which circumstance makes her the more artful in deceiving strangers. It is believed she has gone toward New Orleans, or may be secreted by persons along the river road.

All masters of vessels, ferrymen, and others are hereby cautioned against harboring or carrying off said woman, under penalty of the law. Whoever will apprehend and lodge her in any jail so that I may get her again shall receive the above reward, with reasonable charges paid.

**ELIZABETH YOUNG.**  
Young Place, Assumption Parish, La.  
October 18, 1849.
